---
title: "Progress Reporting"
---
This is the practice of sharing regular updates about the current status of your work. It provides visibility to others regarding which tasks are finished, what is currently being worked on, and what is coming next.

### Project status reports
This strategy involves the regular distribution of structured updates to stakeholders, documenting the overall health, progress, and performance of a project over a specific reporting period. These summaries typically compare actual achievements against the baseline plan, tracking key performance metrics, budget expenditures, and schedule variances. This framework serves as an official record to flag emerging risks, highlight key milestones achieved, and align cross-functional teams on upcoming priorities.

### Stand-ups
This strategy involves conducting brief, high-frequency synchronization meetings—held multiple times per week—where team members share concise updates to maintain continuous momentum. Participants outline the tasks they completed since the last sync, the items they intend to focus on next, and any active obstacles blocking their progress. This framework ensures rapid informational alignment, promotes collective accountability, and allows teams to identify and address impediments early in the execution cycle through regular, time-limited touchpoints.

### Progress review meetings
This strategy involves scheduling formal, periodic checkpoints where the project team and key stakeholders evaluate overall project performance against strategic goals. Unlike high-frequency operational syncs, these sessions focus on broader milestones, budget tracking, resource allocation, and the evaluation of completed deliverables. This framework provides an analytical space to review variances between planned and actual progress, address systemic roadblocks, and make high-level adjustments to the project trajectory.

### RAG Status (Red-Amber-Green)
This strategy involves using a traffic-light visual system to immediately communicate the health, urgency, and performance level of a project, workstream, or specific task. Each color corresponds to a defined state of stability: Green indicates execution is proceeding smoothly on schedule and budget, Amber warns of emerging issues or variances that require close monitoring, and Red flags critical blocks or deviations that require immediate intervention. This framework simplifies complex reporting data into an easily digestible format, allowing stakeholders to quickly identify where resources and leadership support are most urgently needed.

### Kanban Board
This strategy involves using a dynamic, continuous-flow visual board to map out and track the real-time progress of individual work items through a defined process. Tasks are represented as visual cards that move sequentially through vertical columns—typically representing stages like "To Do," "In Progress," and "Done." By enforcing strict work-in-progress (WIP) limits on individual columns, this framework visualizes capacity bottlenecks, surfaces workflow inefficiencies, and provides the team with immediate clarity on operational status and delivery bottlenecks.

### Project Dashboard
This strategy involves consolidating multi-layered project data into a centralized, real-time visual interface that tracks high-level progress and performance metrics. By aggregating diverse data points—such as task completion rates, budget consumption, resource utilization, and timeline health—into scannable charts and indicators, this framework translates complex operational details into immediate, actionable insights. This allows project managers and executives to monitor variance, identify trends, and make data-driven decisions at a single glance.

### Burndown chart
This strategy involves using a graphical representation to track the amount of work remaining in a project or time-limited iteration against the time available to complete it. The chart typically features a downward-sloping "ideal work remaining" line as a baseline, plotted alongside the actual remaining effort—often measured in hours or story points—over successive days. This framework provides teams with an immediate, data-driven visualization of their current velocity, making it easy to see if they are on track to meet their deadline or if the scope needs adjustment.

### Milestone tracking
This strategy involves identifying and monitoring a chronological sequence of major, zero-duration checkpoints that signify the completion of critical phases or key deliverables within a project lifecyle. Instead of tracking day-to-day task execution, this framework focuses on high-level achievements—such as signing a contract, finishing a prototype, or passing a compliance audit—to evaluate health and velocity. This provides stakeholders with a clear, macro-level view of project health and timeline predictability without getting bogged down in minor operational details.

### Milestone Mini-Retros
This strategy involves conducting brief, focused reflection sessions immediately following the achievement of a major project checkpoint or phase completion. Unlike comprehensive, end-of-project retrospectives, these targeted sessions evaluate what went well, what fell short, and what was learned during that specific phase of execution. This framework allows teams to capture immediate insights while memories are fresh, enabling them to make rapid, iterative adjustments to processes, tools, and collaboration strategies for the remaining project timeline.
